# Conveyancers should contact clients 'even if there are no updates'

By [John Hyde](https://www.lawgazette.co.uk/john-hyde/3670.bio)1 April 2026

The number of conveyancing complaints can be more easily contained if lawyers improve their communication throughout the buying process, the legal ombudsman has advised.

In the third quarter of 2025/26 the ombudsman received 647 complaints relating to residential conveyancing, 18% more than the same period last year. Residential conveyancing now accounts for 36% of complaints accepted by LeO and is by far its biggest source of work.

While the figure is only a tiny fraction of the 1.1 million residential property transactions completed in 2024/25, the financially stretched ombudsman service is anxious to reduce its workload.

### **Read more**

- _[LSB blocks 11% budget boost for legal ombudsman and warns current model is ‘unsustainable’](https://www.lawgazette.co.uk/news/lsb-set-to-block-11-budget-boost-for-ombudsman/5126300.article)_
- _[Conveyancing: law firms told to prepare for surge in stamp duty complaints as April deadline looms](https://www.lawgazette.co.uk/news/conveyancing-firms-warned-prepare-for-complaints-spike/5122699.article)_

A new article on the LeO website sets out tips to help lawyers strengthen communication, reduce avoidable complaints, and protect consumers and firms. It states that the key drivers of complaints are generally issues with communication, unclear or unrealistic expectations, and delays that are either unjustified or not explained.

Advert

LeO said it recognises that conveyancing lawyers are working in high-pressure environments and face a high workload, and that delay complaints can often be the result of third parties not acting quickly enough. But the complaints-handler stressed that firms should be staying in touch with clients even during periods where no progress is being made, as that is often from where complaints may stem. Periods of silence can be interpreted as lack of progress and leave consumers anxious or frustrated, leading to complaints or repeated queries, LeO said.

‘We recognise that providing updates when there is no substantive progress can feel difficult to prioritise alongside active legal work, particularly when delays sit outside the conveyancer’s control. However, insight shows that short, predictable updates - even when there is nothing new to report - can improve consumer satisfaction, prevent escalation and reduce the volume of incoming queries over time.’

The ombudsman said that while the average duration of a property purchase in 2024 was 17 weeks - twice the time clients typically expect. Lawyers are urged to give clear information at the outset and reduce unrealistic or unclear expectations.

‘When expectations are set clearly at the outset, many service providers find this reduces reactive chasing, repeat explanations, and improves consumer experience, which reduces the potential for complaints,’ said the ombudsman. ‘While early conversations can feel time intensive, they often help to ensure that the service provider’s resources can be used to progress the transaction, which is particularly important in high volume caseloads.’

Although I have been a Lexcel assessor for around 15 years, I was a residential conveyancer for longer than that. I do know how hard it is to meet client expectations and the feeling of hopelessness when you have done your absolute best for someone - and it still isn't apparently good enough.




Lawyers won't want to acknowledge that LeO knows anything - but the advice is right. I see the complaints registers of tens of law firms and some are very good at categorising the nature of complaints they receive. It's pretty much always about 'delay', 'failure to follow instructions', 'unexpected costs' - issues which are under a firm's control. They then try to improve their procedures. Lexcel is obviously a voluntary standard - no-one makes you have it. But, the documentation relating to the standard is on The Law Society website. As an exercise, have a look at sections 6.2 and 6.4 of Lexcel - do you cover all of the issues raised by those sections in your client care documentation? If not, redraft them and tackle the thorny issues such as 6.2f - "establish in what timescale the matter will be dealt with" - yes it can be done.




The person phoning the client now and again doesn't have to be the lawyer handling the transaction - experienced secretaries and paralegals can make contact and give an effective update. Build the calls into your workflow.




"When expectations are set clearly at the outset, many service providers find this reduces reactive chasing, repeat explanations, and improves consumer experience, which reduces the potential for complaints,’ said the ombudsman. "




Residential conveyancing will never be a perfect process - but it is possible to take control of a difficult situation.

Leo is part of a regulatory architecture that has badly failed. Politicians in 2007 passed legislation that was badly drawn, internally inconsistent and contradictory. Furthermore, it eroded the independence of the legal profession.




Conveyancers have been badly let down by their leaders and now they must become tax advisers and environmental scientists on top of being AML, company law and trust law experts.




On a human level, conveyancers are leaving the sector in droves. And they are angry. I have seen decent, hardworking property lawyers in despair as to how toxic conveyancing has become. This has meant mental health issues and ‘burnout’. I saw one solicitor simply walk out the door of his branch office he had managed for 25 years- never to return. A broken man. Several colleagues speak of being ‘hollowed out’.




The reasons for the above state of affairs are legion and they are not just external ones. Some law firms have lost sight of their ethical roots and are obsessed with crude targets. This was not what motivated most solicitors to enter the profession. Other law firms have fallen into the trap of treating conveyancing like a product or commodity, to be dealt with on a digital production line. This undermines professionalism and encourages a greedy law tech sector to lobby government to take conveyancing over.




Add to the above poisonous mix unregulated estate agents chasing constantly and unrealistic expectations there is little time for reflection or doing the work professionally . But the LeO still expects property lawyers to find the time to say to clients ‘nothing to report’.
